This verse announces that the Hour, meaning the Resurrection, has drawn near, and that the moon has been split. The commentators present these as signs meant to awaken people to the nearness of the afterlife. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy explain that the splitting of the moon actually happened during the Prophet's ﷺ time in Mecca, before the Hijra, in answer to the Quraysh's demand for a sign: the moon split into two parts, one above the mountain and the other behind it, and the Prophet ﷺ said, 'Bear witness.' They rely on reports from Ibn Mas'ud, Anas, Ibn 'Abbas and Jubayr ibn Mut'im. Al-Mawardi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and others report a minority view, attributed to al-Hasan and 'Ata', that the verb refers to the future and the splitting will occur on the Day of Resurrection; most scholars reject this, pointing to the past tense and the following verses. Ibn 'Ashur, al-Shinqiti and al-Sha'rawi discuss the matter further, offering natural explanations or stressing that the miracle was a single sign.

Regarding the next verse, 'And if they see a sign, they turn away and say: a passing magic,' Mujahid and Qatada understand 'passing, fading away,' while Abu al-'Aliya, al-Dahhak and al-Akhfash take it to mean 'firm and strongly twisted.' The following verses speak of their denial and their following of desires, that every matter reaches its settled end, and that the Quran contains accounts of past peoples that should deter them, yet warnings no longer avail. The passage closes with the Day when people rise from their graves with humbled eyes, like scattered locusts, hastening toward the caller, while the disbelievers say: this is a hard day.

This verse describes the disbelievers' reaction: when they see a sign that proves the Prophet's truthfulness, they turn away and call it continuous magic. The commentators differ on the meaning of "mustamirr". Mujahid, Qatada, al-Farra, al-Kisa'i and al-Tabari take it to mean passing and fading away, so the magic will soon vanish, while Abu al-'Aliya and al-Dahhak understand it as strong and firmly twisted, from the image of a tightly braided rope. Others, including al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, prefer the sense of lasting and continuous, since the signs kept following one another, or of bitter and repugnant. All link the verse to the splitting of the moon in Mecca during the Prophet's lifetime, reported through Anas, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and others, when the Meccans questioned travellers who had also seen it. Al-Baghawi mentions an isolated view that the splitting will happen on the Day of Resurrection, but most scholars reject it because the verse speaks of a past event. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur note that this habit of rejecting every sign shows that the disbelievers follow their desires rather than the truth, while Qutb sees it as stubbornness in the face of the signs of the universe.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the Quraysh who denied the Prophet ﷺ after seeing clear signs, following their desires rather than the truth. The phrase “every matter is settled” means, they say, that every affair, good or bad, reaches an end where it comes to rest. Qatada, Muqatil and al-Kalbi hold that good remains with its people in Paradise and evil with its people in Hellfire, or that every statement has a reality and a final outcome that will appear in this world or the next. Al-Farra' adds that the rejection and the belief each remain until every party knows the truth of its state through reward or punishment. Ibn Kathir and al-Sam'ani take it to mean the lasting reward of the believers and the punishment of the disbelievers. Al-Razi allows both a warning to the deniers and a consolation for the Prophet, or the fixity of the matter in God's knowledge. The commentators agree that falsehood vanishes and truth endures. Most affirm that the splitting of the moon happened in the Prophet's lifetime as a miracle, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report, while al-Hasan and some others place it on the Day of Resurrection, a view Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya reject. Abu Hayyan and al-Zamakhshari discuss the readings of “mustaqirr” with fatha or kasra, and Abu Hatim finds no justification for the fatha. Ibn 'Ashur reads the verse as a promise that the Prophet's call will firmly settle after being shaken. Thus, according to these commentaries, the verse warns the deniers and steadies the believers.

The commentators explain that the reports that came to the people of Mecca, namely the accounts of earlier nations who denied their prophets and suffered punishment, contain enough to restrain them from denial and error, and that this is a perfect and complete wisdom. Most of them take these reports to be the Quranic stories of past peoples. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand the word mizdajar as a restraint or a point of deterrence, while Mujahid takes it to mean an end, and Ibn Atiyya widens the reports to include exhortations, stories and examples of punishment. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi treat the word as a noun of action or of place, and several note that the form derives from an original root with a t that became d. As for the particle ma that follows, al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan take it as a negation, meaning that warnings do no good, whereas al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Ashur read it as a rebuking question. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di attribute their failure to benefit to God's decree of wretchedness upon them. The commentators present these views side by side without choosing between them.

The commentators explain that this verse follows the account of the Quraysh rejecting the sign of the splitting of the moon and following their desires. They agree that the reports of earlier nations in the Quran contain what should deter people from disbelief, and that the Quran is a perfect and complete wisdom. The phrase "fa-ma tughni al-nudhur" means, according to al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan, that warnings are of no use to those who persist in denial; al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi also allow it to be read as a question, namely "what use are warnings?" Opinions differ on the grammar of "hikmatun baligha": al-Tabari, al-Zajjaj, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan treat it as a substitute for "ma", al-Tabari and al-Nahhas also allow it as the predicate of an implied subject, and al-Zamakhshari records a reading in the accusative as a circumstantial clause. Al-Zamakhshari takes "mazdajar" to mean a place of restraint, whereas al-Mawardi understands it as what prevents sins. Ibn Kathir, al-Biqa'i and Ibn Sa'di draw from the verse that guidance and misguidance belong to God, so warnings do not benefit those whom He has destined for misery. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the Quranic reports are a stronger proof than the splitting of the moon. The meaning most commentators hold is that the perfect wisdom is the Quran, and that warnings do not reach the stubborn who refuse.

God tells His Prophet ﷺ in this verse to turn away from the polytheists, whom warnings no longer reach, and to wait for the day when the caller, identified by most commentators as Israfil, calls people toward a terrible and unfamiliar matter, namely the Standing and its horrors. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir understand turning away as ceasing to argue with them and being patient, whereas al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi read it as withdrawing from intercession or debate. Al-Nasafi, Abu al-Su'ud and Ibn Juzayy take the caller to be Israfil, while al-Razi also mentions Gabriel or an angel appointed for the task. Al-Mawardi lists six meanings of muhti'in, including hastening, gazing and stretching the neck, and several early scholars echo these. The commentators agree that nukr means frightful and unfamiliar, and that the readings nukr and nukr differ without conflict in meaning. On the reading of khushsha'an versus khashi'an, al-Tabari and Abu Hayyan explain the singular form in terms of usage attested in Ibn Mas'ud's codex, while al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur accept the grammatical latitude. Lowered gazes signal humiliation, and the image of scattered locusts, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur explain, expresses both multitude and confusion. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir report that the disbelievers will say that this is a hard day, which Ibn Sa'di notes is easy for believers.

This verse describes the state of people on the Day of Resurrection, when the Caller summons them to a terrible and frightful matter. They come out of their graves with humbled eyes, like scattered locusts, rushing toward the Caller, while the disbelievers say: this is a hard day. The commentators agree that khushu' means humiliation and abasement, and that the eyes are singled out because they show a person's honour or disgrace. Al-Tabari notes that the eyes stand for the whole body. Al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir and al-Mawardi identify the Caller as Israfil, while al-Zamakhshari allows either Israfil or Gabriel. Most explain the simile of the locusts as a picture of great numbers and surging movement. Al-Razi, Abu Hayyan and al-Baghawi, however, see two stages: first a confused crowd like moths, then a purposeful march toward the gathering like locusts. The readings differ: khushsha'an in the plural, khashi'an in the singular, and khashi'ah in the feminine. Abu Hatim prefers the singular, supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, while al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayda consider all forms permissible. On how the verse connects to what precedes it, al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi treat the pause after 'turn away from them' as complete and link the time phrase to the verb 'come out', whereas Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan attach it to an implied verb. Al-Nahhas and Ibn 'Atiyya regard the command to turn away as abrogated by the verse of fighting, while Ibn 'Ashur reads it as consolation for the Prophet ﷺ alone.

This verse describes the Day of Resurrection, when the caller summons people to a dreadful matter. They come out of their graves with lowered gaze, like scattered locusts, rushing toward the caller with necks outstretched, and the disbelievers say: this is a hard day. The commentators agree on this general meaning. On the word muhti'in, al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and Ibn Atiyya report several readings: hastening according to Abu Ubayda, coming forward according to al-Dahhak, intending the call according to Qatada, gazing fixedly according to Ibn Abbas, and opening the ears to the sound according to Ikrima. Al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir stress the idea of speed. Most identify the caller as Israfil. On khushsha'an, the readers differ: Abu Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read khashi'an in the singular, while the majority read the plural, and al-Farra' holds that both are permitted. The commentators explain that the eyes are singled out because humility shows most clearly there. As for the phrase a hard day, al-Razi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Kathir state that it is a day of great terror for the disbelievers, and al-Razi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi note that attributing the words to the disbelievers implies that the believers do not face the same hardship.

This verse states that the people of Noah denied their prophet before the people of Muhammad ﷺ, calling his servant Noah a liar, saying he was mad, and driving him away with abuse. The commentators differ on the meaning of the word "was driven away." Mujahid, followed by Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi, takes it to mean that he was struck with madness or seized by jinn. Ibn Zayd, cited by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, understands it as threats and insults, relying on the verse "If you do not desist, O Noah, you will be stoned." Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi see the phrase as continuing the speech of his people, meaning he was repelled by force and threatened with death. All agree that the verse consoles the Prophet and warns the Quraysh. When Noah despaired of his people, he asked his Lord for victory, and God answered him with the flood. Al-Qurtubi notes that prophets only call for the destruction of their people with God's permission. Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and Ibn Uthaymin see the title "Our servant" as a mark of honour. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Ashur also explain the repetition of the verb "denied" as emphasis, and Ibn Ashur explains the passive form as avoiding naming the agent.

The commentators place this verse within the story of Noah, peace be upon him, and see its purpose as consoling the Prophet ﷺ and warning the Quraysh about the fate of nations who denied their messengers. Noah's people denied their servant Noah, called him mad, and abused him with insults and threats. When he despaired of their faith, he prayed to his Lord, saying that he was overpowered by them and asking Him to take vengeance. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Atiyya agree that the prayer was a request for punishment, and that God answered it with the flood. Most readers pronounce anni with a fatha, meaning 'because I am overcome', while the Basran grammarians, such as Sibawayh and al-Zajjaj, read it with a kasra, understanding an implied verb of saying. As for the meaning of fantasir, the majority take it as a request for God to avenge Noah on his people; Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan report the view that it means victory for God and His religion, while some Sufis read it as a struggle against Noah's own self, an opinion Ibn Atiyya considers less convincing. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi relate that one of his opponents would seize him by the throat until he fainted, after which he would revive and pray for his people. Ibn Ashur sees the word maghlub as a metaphor for despair.

This verse describes the flood that drowned Noah's people, after Noah had called on his Lord against them when he despaired of their faith. The commentators agree on the general meaning: the sky opened with abundant, continuous water, the earth burst forth in springs, and the water of the sky met the water of the earth by a decree God had determined. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand this as a very heavy and intense rain, while Ibn Abbas, as reported by several of them, said the rain lasted about forty days. As for the "gates of heaven", most, including al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi, take it as a figure for rain so heavy that it seems to pour from gates, whereas Ali ibn Abi Talib identified them with the Milky Way, called the "crack of the sky". Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn Abbas understood an actual opening.

The meaning of "a matter already decreed" is also discussed. Muqatil holds that the water of the sky and that of the earth were equal in amount, Qatada that God had decreed their drowning, and al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir that it was an order written in the Preserved Tablet. Al-Tabari notes that the singular verb "met" refers here to two kinds of water. The ark is described as made of planks; the commentators differ on the "nails": Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada say they are nails, al-Hasan and Ikrima the prow that cuts the waves, and Mujahid also the ribs of the ship. On "before Our eyes", most read divine protection, while some read command or revelation.

The verse describes the punishment of Noah's people after they rejected his message: God opened the gates of heaven to a pouring rain and caused the earth to gush forth in springs, so that the water of the sky and the water of the earth met according to a decree already determined, which was the destruction of that people by the flood. The commentators agree that the water here has two sources, from heaven and from the earth, and that the singular form is read as a collective noun. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the rain lasted forty days, while a report from Ibn Abbas cited by Ibn Kathir says it fell without clouds. On the meaning of 'munhamir', as-Suddi says abundant, while al-Mubarrad and Ibn Qutayba say it means pouring forth vigorously. As for 'opening the gates of heaven', most read it as an image of heavy rain, whereas a report from Ali identifies it with the Milky Way, which he calls the seam of the sky. On 'qudira' (decreed), Ibn Qutayba understands the two waters to have been equal in measure, Qatada takes it to mean that drowning was decreed for them, and al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi take it as written in the Preserved Tablet; al-Qurtubi cites Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi that destiny precedes trial. All identify the vessel of 'planks and fastenings' with Noah's ship; opinions differ on the fastenings (nails according to Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Zayd), the prow that cleaves the water (al-Hasan and Ikrima), or the ribs of the ship (Mujahid). 'Sailing before Our eyes' is understood as divine protection and care, and 'as a recompense for one who had been rejected' refers, for most, to Noah rejected by his people, while Ibn Abbas and Mujahid take it to mean God Himself.

This verse describes how God carried Noah on a vessel made of planks and fastenings, after He had opened the gates of heaven with pouring rain and caused the earth to gush forth springs. The ship sailed under God's watchful eye. The commentators agree that the planks are the broad timbers of the hull. The word dusur, plural of dissar, is understood by most of them as nails or pegs that fasten the planks, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi report. Al-Hasan, Ikrima and, in one report, Ibn Abbas, take it to mean the prow that pushes through the water. Mujahid says it refers to the ribs or crossbeams, and al-Dahhak to its ends and base. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya record these senses as well. On the meaning of the phrase 'a reward for one who was disbelieved', opinions differ. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd take it that God is the one who was rejected, while most take it that Noah was the one rejected by his people. Al-Tabari concludes that the event was both a punishment for the people and a reward for Noah. Ibn Ashur notes that naming the ship only by its features is a rhetorical device. Ibn Kathir adds that the event and the ship remain a sign for people to reflect upon. Readers differ slightly in pronunciation, but this does not change the meaning.

The verse describes the ark on which God carried Noah, built of planks and fastened with pins, sailing under God's eyes and His protection. The commentators explain that it was a recompense. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most scholars take the word refers to Noah, whose people rejected his prophethood, so God avenged him and rewarded his patience. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd, followed by Ibn Juzayy, understand it to refer to God Himself, so that the drowning is a punishment for their disbelief in Him. Al-Tabari judges the view that it refers to Noah to be the more sound, while other readings with the verb in the active voice point toward the disbelievers. Al-Razi notes the recompense concerns the rejection of Noah rather than his gratitude, and several commentators, including al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur, note that Noah was himself a blessing that his people denied. The scholars agree that this passage belongs to the account of the flood and serves as a warning to the Quraysh.

This verse says that God left the ship in which He saved Noah and those with him as a sign and a lesson for the peoples who came after Noah's people, so that they would take heed and not follow their path of disbelief and rejection of the messengers. The question "Is there anyone who will remember?" is an urging to reflection and admonition.

The commentators differ on what the pronoun "We left it" refers to. Qatada says God preserved the ship's remains at Baqirdа in the Jazira region, or on al-Judi for a long time, until the early members of this community saw it. Al-Razi, Abu al-Sud and Ibn Juzayy take it as referring to the ship or to the event itself, while Ibn Ashur explains that "leaving" means preserving the sign, whereas the sura of al-Ankabut says "We made it a sign" about its construction. Ibn Uthaymin suggests the pronoun may refer to the kind of ship, so the sign is the making of such vessels.

They also differ on the meaning of "mudakkir". Ibn Zayd takes it as one who remembers and takes heed, Qatada and Matar al-Warraq as one who seeks good or knowledge so that he may be helped, and Muhammad ibn Ka'b as one who restrains himself from sins. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Tabari report a reading with a doubled dal transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, which al-Tabari also links to an Arabic usage, and the word comes from an original form "mudtakir".

Most commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Sa'di, connect this verse with the next one, which states that God made the Qur'an easy for remembrance. They explain that He made it easy to recite, memorise and understand, and Ibn Sa'di adds that it is wholly easy for whoever applies himself to it.

This passage recounts how God destroyed the people of Noah after they denied His servant, called him mad and drove him away. Noah prayed to his Lord that he be helped, and God answered by opening the gates of heaven to a pouring rain and making the earth gush with springs, so that the two waters met as had been decreed. Noah and those with him were carried on the ship of planks and fastenings as a reward for his patience, and the commentators say God left the ship as a sign for people to reflect upon. They agree on the severity of the punishment and the clarity of the warning. They differ, however, on several points. Ibn Zayd and Ibn Kathir take the phrase 'wa-zdujira' as God's words meaning that they rebuked him, whereas Mujahid takes it as the words of his people, meaning he was possessed. On the 'dusur', Qatada, al-Qurazi, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Jubayr say they are the fastening pegs, al-Hasan and Ikrima say the prow that cuts the water, and Mujahid says the ribs of the ship. As for 'the one who was disbelieved', Mujahid and Ibn Zayd take it to mean God, while al-Farra' takes it to mean Noah. On the question 'Is there anyone who will take heed?', Qatada understands one who seeks good, Muhammad ibn Ka'b one who restrains himself from sins, and Mutarrif al-Warraq one who seeks knowledge. Al-Tabari understands the facilitation of the Quran as ease of memorising and learning from it, and Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of the seven modes of recitation to illustrate that ease. The commentators conclude that these verses warn the Quraysh and console the Prophet.

The commentators explain that this verse means God made the Qur'an easy, in both its recitation and its meaning, for whoever wishes to remember and take heed. The question is repeated after each story in the surah to awaken the listener. Most agree that the ease concerns first of all memorization: Sa'id ibn Jubayr says the Qur'an is the only divine book recited entirely from memory, and Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy and al-Razi note that it is retained easily, even by children. As to the sense of remembering, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud take it to mean taking admonition and mending one's ways. Qatada, in a report preserved by al-Tabari, understands instead: is there anyone seeking good who may be helped? Al-Tabari prefers the meaning of admonition as the most apparent. On the reading of the word, Ibn Mas'ud reports that the Prophet had him recite it with a doubled dal, while others read it with a dhal; Abu Hayyan notes that both readings are known. Al-Razi observes that remembrance may be a recalling of a natural disposition buried within a person. The commentators draw no legal ruling from the verse and confine themselves to its exhortative meaning for the reader.

The commentators explain that this verse reports that the people of 'Ad denied their prophet Hud, and that the question "How was My punishment and My warning?" is meant to shock and to stress how great the punishment was, as was the warning that preceded it. The following verses describe that punishment: God sent a violent wind, and the scholars give it closely related meanings. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Dahhak take it to be a bitterly cold wind, Ibn Zayd a very forceful one, and others a wind that makes a loud sound.

As for the "day of ill omen that persisted", Qatada holds that the misfortune kept on until it brought them to Hell, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak take it to mean a bitter day for them, and some report that it was a Wednesday at the end of the month. Al-Mawardi notes that the word "mustamirr" may mean that which passes or that which lasts.

The commentators agree that the wind uprooted people from their places and hurled them on their heads, breaking their necks, so that they looked like uprooted palm trunks. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that some dug pits to shelter in, and the wind pulled them out. Al-Tabari sees an ellipsis in the comparison, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Zajjaj read it as an image of tall bodies without heads. The masculine form of "munqa'ir" is explained by grammarians as a consequence of the word "nakhl" being used both as masculine and feminine.

The verse ends with the repetition of the question and the reminder that the Qur'an has been made easy for remembrance, a repetition which several commentators, Ibn Juzayy among them, read as a way of awakening the listener at each account.

This verse tells that God sent against the people of 'Ad, who denied their prophet Hud, a violent wind in a day of continuous misfortune. The wind uprooted people, threw them onto their heads so that their necks broke, and left them like uprooted palm trunks. On the meaning of "sarsar", al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others, following Qatada and al-Dahhak, take it to mean a cold wind, while Ibn Zayd takes it to mean a very strong wind, and others see a wind that makes a piercing sound. As for the "day of misfortune", most commentators read it as a day of ill omen and severity for them, and several report that it was a Wednesday at the end of the month, whereas others do not tie it to one specific day but to a whole period in which their punishment unfolded. Qatada adds that this misfortune continued until it led them to Hell, and al-Hasan and al-Dahhak say it was bitter for them. On the image of the palm trunks, Ibn 'Abbas speaks of the roots, al-Dahhak of the trunks' lower parts, and Mujahid of heads severed from bodies, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan understand the comparison as the fall of lifeless, tall and heavy bodies. The commentators explain the repetition of the question about the punishment as a way to strike the heart, and the mention of the ease of the Qur'an for remembrance as a call to reflect.

This verse describes the wind sent against the people of 'Ad: it plucks people from their places and hurls them down, so that they lie like uprooted palm trunks. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most commentators explain sarsar as a cold, violent wind, while Ibn Zayd and al-Mawardi understand it as a very fierce wind or one that makes a howling sound. The day of misfortune is generally taken to be a day of calamity for 'Ad; Qatada adds that the misfortune continued until it brought them to Hell, and Ibn 'Abbas and others report that it was a Wednesday at the end of the month, a report Ibn 'Atiyya considers weak. Al-Qurtubi reconciles this with the tradition about Wednesday by saying the day was unlucky only for the disbelievers. The commentators agree that the wind tore heads from bodies or threw men onto their heads. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi report that the people of 'Ad were very tall, which is why they are compared to palm trunks. On the grammatical gender of nakhl, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi note it can be treated as masculine or feminine, and here the choice follows the rhyme. Al-Razi, Ibn 'Ashur and al-Biqa'i offer different readings of the state of the bodies. Ibn 'Uthaymin notes the agreement on the violence and suddenness of the destruction, without settling the details.

This verse belongs to the account of 'Ad, the people of Hud, who denied their prophet. It asks, in a tone of wonder and warning, how Allah's punishment and warning turned out. The commentators explain that God sent upon them a violent wind which was cold according to Qatada, al-Dahhak and Ibn 'Abbas, while al-Tabari and Ibn Zayd describe it as very forceful, and others as one whose howling could be heard. They say it was a day of continuous misfortune; Qatada holds that the ill omen persisted until it brought them to Hell, while al-Dahhak says it was bitter for them. Al-Kisa'i mentions a view that the word comes from bitterness. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that the wind lasted about seven nights and eight days. The commentators agree that the wind uprooted people from their places and hurled them onto their heads, leaving bodies like uprooted palm trunks. They differ on the meaning of 'a'jaz': Ibn 'Abbas says the roots, al-Dahhak the hindquarters. The comparison is explained either by heads separating from bodies or by the pits in which they had hidden. Some add that the wind pulled them out of their graves. The question is repeated to heighten the awe and warning, as al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur note. The verse ends with the Qur'an being made easy for remembrance, which al-Tabari and others link to memorising and reflecting upon it.

This verse states that God made the Qur'an easy for remembrance and asks whether anyone will take heed. Al-Tabari explains that it was made facilitated and accessible for whoever wishes to be mindful and admonished, a reading echoed by Ibn Sa'di, al-Jaza'iri and the Tafsir al-Muyassar, which connect the ease both to recitation and memorization and to understanding its meanings. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Uthaymin see the repetition after each story as an encouragement to remember and reflect on the Qur'an. Ibn 'Ashur notes it repeats a similar verse in the story of Noah, while al-Razi explains that the singular punishment and plural warnings reflect the priority of mercy over wrath.

The surrounding context is the people of 'Ad. The commentators agree that the wind was violent and that its adjective sarsar meant cold, according to Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Dahhak, or loud, according to others. Most identify the ill-omened day as a Wednesday, as reported by al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, though Abu Hayyan holds that it refers to a period rather than a particular day. Al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari describe how the wind uprooted people and threw them down on their heads, so that they looked like felled palm trunks.

The commentators differ on some words. Su'ur was read as torment by Ibn 'Abbas, hardship by Qatada, madness by al-Farra' and distance from the truth by Wahb. Readings of the word ashir also vary, as Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Atiyya note. Still, all agree on the core point: the people denied their prophet and were punished.

The verse states that the people of Thamud, the people of Salih, denied the warnings that came to them, which most commentators take to mean the messengers. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that their objection was that a single man among them should be followed by a large community, and that a mere human should claim to receive revelation. Al-Zamakhshari adds that their scorn also targeted the fact that the messenger was a man rather than an angel. Al-Razi distinguishes between reading nudhur as the plural of nadhir, which makes the rejection of Salih a rejection of all prophets, and reading it as warnings in the sense of the signs and admonitions they received. As for the word su'ur, the commentators differ: Ibn Abbas, Qatada and al-Hasan take it to mean punishment or hardship, al-Farra and Ibn Qutayba madness, Wahb and Mujahid straying far from the truth, al-Suddi burning, and Sufyan ibn Uyayna the plural of sa'ir, a blazing fire. They then accuse him of being a liar and an arrogant man, and God answers that tomorrow they will know who the liar and the insolent one is, a reading that varies between the taa and the yaa. The commentators connect this passage with the story of the she-camel, the sharing of water, her slaughter by Qudar ibn Salif, and the cry that destroyed them until they became like the dry brushwood of a livestock pen, a term whose meaning is debated between burnt bones, crumbling dust from walls, and grass trampled by animals.

This verse reports that the people of Thamud denied the warnings brought by their prophet Salih and exclaimed in disbelief: how can we follow a single man of our own kind when we are a large multitude? They add that following him would put us in error and in hardship, or in madness according to the interpretations. The commentators agree on the core meaning: they reject that a prophet should be an isolated mortal with no supporters, and they find it strange that he alone among them should receive revelation. The meaning of the word su'ur is disputed. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Ibn Kathir take it as punishment or its severity, Qatada as hardship, al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba as madness, Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna as the plural of sa'ir, meaning flames, Mujahid as distance from the truth, and al-Sudi as burning. According to al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and others, Salih had warned them of error and fire, and they turned his words back on him, saying that if they followed him they would be just what he described. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that the nominative reading of bashar is admitted, although the accusative is the better-known reading. Al-Razi observes that the phrasing emphasises human nature and the prophet's solitude as the grounds for refusal, rather than following as such. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi see the verse as part of a brief account of their arrogance, which they used to disparage the prophet's claim to be above them.

This verse records the Thamud's rejection of their prophet Salih, peah whom they found it hard to accept that one man from among them should receive the revelation: "Has the Reminder been cast upon him from among us?" God replies that their charge is that he is a "liar and insolent" (kadhdhab ashir), and that they will know tomorrow who the liar and the insolent one is. Commentators agree that "ashir" means arrogant, boastful, and overbearing, and that the accusation is that he wanted to lord it over them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that the readings with "you will know" and "they will know" are both correct and close in meaning, the first being Salih's address to his people, the second a divine announcement. As for "tomorrow", al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir relate it to the Day of Judgment, while Ibn Juzayy and others take it to be the moment the punishment strikes in this world, since Arabic uses "tomorrow" for any near or future time. The word "su'ur" is explained in several ways: torment according to Ibn Abbas, hardship according to Qatada, madness according to al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba, and error according to Wahb. Al-Razi and Ibn Ashur analyse the rhetoric as a step-by-step expression of disbelief, while Ibn Uthaymin sees these objections as baseless, since being human does not prevent someone from being a messenger. The commentators then move on to the story of the she-camel and the punishment that struck the people.

This verse announces that the people of Thamud, to whom the prophet Salih was sent, will learn tomorrow who the arch-liar and the insolent one really is, whether Salih or themselves. The commentators explain that "tomorrow" refers either to the moment the punishment strikes them in this world or to the Day of Judgment. The threat answers their earlier protest, in which they wondered why a revelation should descend upon one of them and called him a liar and a boaster. Al-Tabari notes that the readings with the second person and the third person are close in meaning and both valid. The commentators explain "ashir" as arrogant, boastful, overbearing, and exuberant, and al-Mawardi adds the sense of one who does not care what he says. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan record a reading with a fatha on the shin and a shadda on the ra, which would be a superlative meaning "the greatest in wickedness", though Abu Hayyan notes it is rarely used in Arabic. Al-Razi observes that the threat may refer to punishment in the hereafter, and that "tomorrow" serves to bring the event close in time. Ibn 'Ashur, by contrast, suggests that "tomorrow" may refer to the day of the Muslims' victory at Badr or the conquest of Mecca, an interpretation he alone holds.

This verse says that God will send forth for the people of Thamud the she-camel they had asked of their prophet Salih, as a trial for them. He tells Salih to watch what they will do and to be patient with their harm, and to inform them that the water is shared between them and the she-camel, each having a turn. The commentators agree that fitna means a test, and that the camel was a miracle brought out of the rock through Salih's prayer, as al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and al-Jalalayn report. On how the sharing worked, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, following Mujahid, explain that the camel drank the water on one day while the people took her milk on the other, while Muqatil holds that the camel came to the water on the day they did not. Ibn Atiyya takes the division to mean that the two parties are equal on the day the camel does not come. Al-Razi notes that the verb is in the present tense to confirm that the event is certain, and he sees the trial as the miracle itself, since it separates believers from deniers. Most commentators, including Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, name the killer as Qudar ibn Salif, and relate that the camel was slaughtered and that Gabriel's single cry destroyed the people.

This verse tells the prophet Salih to inform his people, Thamud, that the water is shared between them and the she-camel, which God brought out of the rock as a sign and a trial. She has one day of drinking and they have another, and each share is attended by the one it belongs to. The commentators agree on a rotation of shares. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the camel has her day and the people theirs. The pronoun 'between them' is masculine because rational beings take precedence over animals, as noted by al-Tabari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy. Mujahid says Thamud came for water on the camel's absent day and for milk on the day she came, while Muqatil holds that the camel came to drink on their absent day. Al-Razi offers several possible reasons for the division, including the camel's great size frightening other animals, or the scarcity of water. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi understand 'muhtadar' as meaning each share is attended by its owner, and Ibn Kathir adds that whoever lacks his turn is kept from it. The commentators do not decide between these readings and mainly keep the idea of alternating shares of water.

The commentators explain that the Thamud, after God had given them the she-camel as a sign to their prophet Salih and had divided the water between her and them by turns, grew tired of this arrangement. They called upon their companion Qudar ibn Salif, who struck the she-camel with his sword or his hand and killed her. The exegetes agree that one man struck the blow but that the whole people, who consented to it, are counted as responsible; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report this sense, and Abu Hayyan notes that the deed was passed from one to another before Qudar took it on. The punishment was a single cry, which most identify as the cry of Gabriel. Opinions differ on the meaning of “kahashim al-muhtazir”: for Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd it is the dry, thorny wood of a livestock pen, crushed and broken; for Ibn Abbas and Qatada it is burnt bones; for Sa'id ibn Jubayr it is the dust falling from a wall. Al-Hasan and Qatada read “al-muhtazar” with a fatha, meaning the place of the enclosure. Ibn Kathir considers Sa'id ibn Jubayr's view an unusual one and prefers that of Ibn Abbas. Al-Zamakhshari and others stress that the whole people was destroyed, with none left alive.

God asks, to stir the heart, how His punishment and His warnings turned out for Thamud after they hamstrung the she-camel. The commentators read the question as an emphatic reminder of the terrible outcome, and as a warning to the Meccans that the same fate awaits those who reject their messenger. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and others report that the one who hamstrung the camel was Qidar ibn Salif, the most wretched of his people, while al-Tabari notes that the punishment came as a single cry. Opinions differ on the phrase 'like the crushed dry thorns of the one who builds a pen': Ibn Abbas and Qatada take it to mean burnt bones, Sa'id ibn Jubayr dust falling from a wall, Ibn Zayd and al-Dahhak dry branches that the Arabs use to fence in their herds, and Mujahid a broken tent. Al-Razi remarks that the interrogative form here serves to explain and magnify, unlike the account of Noah's people whose punishment was universal. All the commentators agree that the destruction was sudden and complete, and that the prophet's warnings were fulfilled.

This verse states that God sent upon Thamud a single cry, which most commentators identify as the cry of Gabriel, and that they were all destroyed, becoming like dry, broken vegetation. The commentators agree on the general sense of annihilation and desiccation, but differ on the exact image. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Dahhak take the broken thing to be burnt bones or burnt wood, while Ibn Zayd, al-Suddi, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand dry branches and thorns that a herdsman gathers to fence his flock, which the sheep trample until they crumble. Sa'id ibn Jubayr understands it as dust falling from a wall, which Ibn Kathir calls a rare opinion. Another report from Ibn 'Abbas says it is grass eaten by goats. Al-Hasan and Qatada read «al-muhtazar» with a fatha, meaning the place of the enclosure, while the majority reading with a kasra means the one who builds the enclosure. Al-Razi notes that hashim in Arabic denotes dry, brittle wood, and that the comparison may mean they lay like corpses for days, or that they piled up on one another like a woodcutter's bundle. Ibn 'Ashur adds that the comparison targets the state of the brushwood before it is woven into the enclosure.

In this verse God states that He has made the Qur'an easy for remembrance and admonition, and asks whether there is anyone who will take heed. The commentators understand this facility to cover both the recitation and memorization of its words and the grasp and reflection on its meaning. Ibn 'Uthaymin reads the question as an invitation that stirs the listener to reflect, while al-Razi and Ibn Kathir present the verse as a conclusion to the accounts of peoples who denied their prophets. Al-Razi explains that the repetition in the surah serves emphasis, whereas Ibn 'Ashur holds that it calls for gratitude and reflection on the Qur'an, since such reflection protects from error and guides to right guidance. Al-Tabari takes remembrance as admonition that leads a person to refrain from what God dislikes, and Qatada, quoted by al-Sam'ani, defines the one who remembers as one who seeks good and is helped to attain it. Commentators place the verse after the story of the people of Lot, who were saved at dawn by a blessing from God. On the general meaning there is broad agreement: the Qur'an is easy to memorize and understand for anyone who seeks instruction, and its call is addressed to everyone who hears it.

This verse in Surah al-Qamar says that the people of Lot rejected the warnings of their prophet, so God sent upon them a storm that pelted them with stones, while Lot and his household were saved at the last part of the night. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others explain that the warnings are the signs and punishment Lot announced, and that the family of Lot means those who followed him in his faith, with many including his daughters. The rescue is described as a blessing from God, granted to those who give thanks through faith and obedience. The commentators differ on the meaning of hasib. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi take it to be stones or pebbles hurled by the wind. Al-Mawardi offers five possible meanings, including clouds, angels or the wind, while al-Razi understands it as a punishment that pelted them and notes that the word can denote a violent wind. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Atiyya place the rescue in the last third of the night, just before dawn. On the word sahar, al-Farra, al-Zajjaj and al-Akhfash explain that it takes tanwin because it is indefinite, and loses it when a specific time is meant. Ibn al-Qayyim develops this grammatical point at length. The commentators do not settle these views and report each as transmitted.

This verse tells that God sent a violent wind against the people of Lot, who had denied their messenger, pelting them with small stones, and that He saved the family of Lot, meaning his household and the believers among them. The commentators agree that this means Lot and his two daughters, and that the rescue took place in the last part of the night, just before dawn. This deliverance is a favour from God, who thus rewards whoever thanks Him, believes and obeys. Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi understand the hasib as a hail of stones or a wind that carries them, while al-Mawardi offers five possible meanings, including clouds, angels or the wind itself. Al-Razi judges that the word refers to a general punishment in which wind, angels, clouds and stones all played a part, and he considers this the most convincing reading. As for sahar, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi take it to mean the end of the night, al-Zamakhshari also mentioning the view that there were two such periods, whereas al-Razi limits it to the last sixth of the night. On the grammar, al-Farra, al-Zajjaj and al-Akhfash explain that the word takes nunation because it is indefinite and does not refer to one particular day. Ibn al-Qayyim notes that the family of Lot can also be read as his followers, while most commentators take it to mean his kin, his daughters and those who believed with him.

The commentators explain that this verse closes the account of the people of Lot by recalling the rescue of Lot's household, which is a blessing from God, and that God rewards in the same way whoever gives thanks through faith and obedience. The people of Lot denied their messenger and his warnings, so God sent upon them a hasib, a wind that pelted them with stones and pebbles, while Lot and his family were saved bi-sahar, that is, in the last part of the night before dawn. al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that the blessing is the deliverance itself, and that the 'family of Lot' are those who believed in him, though al-Baghawi, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi report that this means his two daughters alone. On the meaning of hasib the views differ: al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi take it as stones or a wind that carries them, while others take it as a cloud or angels, as al-Mawardi records.

On the meaning of gratitude, al-Tabari, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Ashur identify it with faith and obedience, al-Qasimi with using the blessing for the purpose it was created for, and Ibn 'Uthaymin with acting in obedience rather than merely speaking. al-Razi notes that deliverance in this world is not necessarily promised, and he prefers the view that the reward is in the Hereafter, while recording the majority opinion that it is a promise to protect the community of Muhammad from general destruction. Ibn 'Ashur sees in the phrase 'from Us' an emphasis on the greatness of this blessing.

Al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and al-Jaza'iri explain that sahar takes nunation because it is indefinite and does not refer to a specific day, and that 'blessing' is either an object of purpose or a verbal noun, as noted by Abu Hayyan, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Nasafi.

This verse says that Lot warned his people of God's punishment, but they doubted his warning and rejected it. The commentators broadly agree on the plain meaning: the verb tamārā, from the root meaning doubt, is understood by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud as disbelief in the warning. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi add that the doubt passed from one person to another, each misleading the others through false arguments. Al-Razi observes that bataša may refer to the punishment that had already occurred, which Lot was threatening, or to the great punishment of the Hereafter; he prefers the first reading because the next verse describes the destruction. The word nudhur is read either as warnings or as warners, as Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note.

The following verse, which recounts the attempt of Lot's people on his guests, the angels in human form, is taken by most exegetes as the continuation of the story. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that Gabriel struck their eyes with his wing, while Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak regard the blinding as a veil that prevented them from seeing the guests. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Su'ud describe the blinding without deciding between these readings. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the oath given here serves to reinforce the lesson addressed to the Quraysh, who had also rejected the Prophet's warnings.

The commentators explain that this verse concerns the people of Lot, who denied his warnings and disputed them, then sought to take his guests, who were angels in the form of handsome men, for the sake of immorality. God then blinded them. For most exegetes, the effacing of their eyes means that the eyes were wiped out and became smooth like the rest of the face. al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that Gabriel struck them with his wing, leaving them wandering and unable to find the door, and al-Tabari cites Ibn 'Abbas that God blinded them so they could not see the guests. al-Razi understands the effacing as a veiling of perception, with the eyes becoming like a smooth surface, and distinguishes this from the verse in Ya-Sin, where it concerns the eyelids. Most agree that the words "taste my punishment and my warnings" are addressed to them through the angels. However, the meaning of tasting differs: al-Mawardi and al-Dahhak take it as a threat of a lesser punishment, while al-Hasan and Qatada take it as a rebuke for the blindness that has struck them. al-Zamakhshari explains that the repetition of the verse in the surah renews reflection and admonition at each account of earlier peoples. al-Razi considers tasting a figure for requital, and warnings to mean what follows from the warning, namely a future punishment. Ibn 'Ashur sees tasting as a metaphor for feeling the punishment, and the warnings as their actual fulfillment.

This verse describes the punishment that struck the people of Lot at dawn, at the beginning of the morning, and which was a lasting torment that did not lift from them. The commentators explain that this punishment consisted of overturning their land so that its upper part became its lower, followed by a rain of stones. Al-Tabari, reporting Ibn Humayd, identifies the time as the break of dawn, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take it as the first part of the day. Al-Razi explains that the word bukra specifies the exact time of the attack, since the verb alone could refer to the whole period from dawn until full daylight. As for the word mustaqirr, al-Tabari, Qatada and Ibn Kathir understand it as a torment that continues into the punishment of the Hereafter, al-Razi takes it to mean a punishment that cannot be averted or lifted, and Ibn 'Ashur describes it as continuous until they were wiped out. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi connect the present torment with the blinding that had just happened, and the repeated phrase taste my punishment and my warnings is read as a rebuke. Al-Zamakhshari sees the repetition as a way of renewing the listener's reflection with each story. On the nature of the blinding, al-Hasan and Qatada say the sight was truly taken away, while Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak speak of a figure of speech, the visitors being hidden from view. Ibn Kathir and Qatada also report the image of Gabriel striking their eyes with his wing. The commentators do not settle between these readings.

The commentators read this verse as a command addressed to the people of Lot after the punishment had struck them: God makes them taste His chastisement and the warnings they were given. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi report that these words were spoken when the punishment came upon them in the morning, namely the overturning of their cities and the rain of baked clay stones. Al-Tabari reports views that the lasting punishment would remain with them until the Day of Resurrection and lead them to the fire of Hell, while Ibn 'Ashur suggests the words may have been cast into their hearts at the arrival of the punishment.

The commentators agree that the verse is a threat and a rebuke to the disbelievers. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur explain that repeating this phrase after each account of the earlier nations is meant to renew the listener's remembrance and awaken him to take heed. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir add that remembering means benefiting from the Qur'an, which God has made easy to understand.

Al-Razi holds that the punishment came twice, one part specific to those who sought to molest the guests and a general one. There is disagreement about the blinding of their eyes: al-Hasan and Qatada take it as real blindness, while al-Dahhak regards it as a veiling of sight without harm to the eyes themselves. On the word bukra, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj explain that it may take tanwin or not depending on whether it means an unspecified morning or a particular one.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to a passage in Surah al-Qamar that repeats after each account of earlier peoples, reflecting on the fate of those who denied their messengers. Its plain meaning is that God has made the Qur'an easy for whoever wants to remember and take heed, so the question is asked: is there anyone who will remember, turn back from what God forbade and do what He commanded. Al-Tabari explains that God made it easy to recall and to be admonished by it.

The commentators broadly agree, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir, that the verse is repeated after each story so that the listener remains alert and mindful. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi compare this repetition to the refrain "Which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?" in Surah al-Rahman, and to "Woe on that day to the deniers" in al-Mursalat. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di stress memorising the Qur'an and reflecting on its meaning.

On the linguistic side, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi render "muddakir" as one who remembers and takes a lesson. Al-Shawkani sees in the repetition an indication of a great blessing that deserves gratitude, while Ibn Ashur sees it as a way of highlighting the Qur'an. Ibn 'Uthaymin notes that the interrogative form is meant to arouse attention.

There is no major disagreement on this verse: all the commentators converge on the idea of a call to reflection and admonition through the Qur'an.

This verse says that the people of Pharaoh, meaning Pharaoh, his household and his leading men, received the warnings from God. Most commentators take the word "warnings" to mean Moses and Aaron together with the signs God gave them: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi identify these with the nine signs, which al-Qurtubi lists. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi understand it to refer to Moses, Aaron and the other prophets, who presented to them what the messengers had warned of. Al-Shawkani, al-Alusi and Ibn 'Ashur read the word as a verbal noun meaning the warning itself. All agree that they denied all these signs, and that God seized them with a mighty and irresistible seizure, which Ibn 'Uthaymin and Ibn Sa'di connect with their drowning in the sea. Ibn Kathir cites an authentic hadith about the Prophet's supplication at Badr and the announcement of the defeat of the assembled forces, and al-Tabari reports that Umar only understood the verse when Badr came. The verses that follow address the Quraysh: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur see in them a warning drawn from the fate of earlier peoples. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi note that the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe than that of this world.

This part of the verse says that Pharaoh's people, meaning Pharaoh, his people and his followers, denied all of God's signs, which most exegetes take to be the nine signs given to Moses. God then seized them with a mighty punishment that no one can overcome, which Ibn Kathir and others identify as drowning. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Ibn Juzayy and al-Mahalli and al-Suyuti understand the warners (al-nudhur) to be Moses, Aaron and the other prophets. Al-Shawkani, Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn 'Uthaymin instead take the word to mean the warnings or signs that Moses delivered to them, and Ibn 'Uthaymin considers this the sounder view. Al-Qurtubi notes that a plural form can refer to two people. As for the pronoun in 'they denied', Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan propose that it refers to all the nations mentioned before, but most commentators apply it to Pharaoh's people. Al-Tabari, Qatada and Ibn 'Ashur explain 'mighty' as one who cannot be overcome in his vengeance and 'powerful' as one whom nothing can resist. Ibn 'Ashur adds that the phrasing stresses the severity of the punishment, as known to the listeners in the case of kings and tyrants. The commentators therefore agree on the general sense of the punishment, but differ on who the messengers were and on what the pronoun refers to.

God addresses the Quraysh of Mecca with a rhetorical question that works as rebuke: are your unbelievers better than those earlier peoples who were destroyed, the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, the people of Lot and Pharaoh's household? Or do you have an exemption written in the Scriptures? The implied answer is no: you are no better, and no immunity is guaranteed. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari read the question as a denial, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi see it as a warning. Most commentators take 'al-zubur' to mean the revealed books, though al-Qurtubi reports Ibn 'Abbas as referring to the Preserved Tablet. On the boast 'we are a united, victorious group', al-Tabari and al-Baghawi understand a confidence in their numbers; God replies that the group will be routed and turn its back, which all commentators link to the battle of Badr, supported by the report of 'Umar and the Prophet leaping in his armour. Al-Razi notes that the address is aimed at those who persist in disbelief and discusses at length what 'better' can mean: strength, rank, or some redeeming quality. Al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir describe the Hour as a trial more dreadful and bitter than the defeat at Badr, a point Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Ashur develop as a warning to a generation that feels safe.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to a rebuke addressed to the Quraysh after the story of earlier peoples such as the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, the people of Lot and the household of Pharaoh. It reports their confident claim that they are a united body that cannot be defeated and will prevail by its strength. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi agree that the divine answer, 'The host will be routed and they will turn their backs', refers to the defeat at Badr. According to Ibn 'Abbas, Ikrima and Qatada, 'Umar did not grasp its meaning until he saw the Prophet ﷺ repeat it, in his armour, on the day of Badr. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir state that the group refers to the Quraysh and that the singular 'the back' is used to match the verse endings.

The scholars differ on the meaning of 'we are a victorious host'. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn al-Jawzi understand a united assembly with one command that cannot be overcome, while al-Kalbi and al-Qurtubi read it as one hand against those who oppose them. Al-Razi explains that the singular 'victorious' follows the word 'host', and that each of them claimed invincibility. Ibn 'Ashur sees the statement as an expression of the polytheists' delusion and as a message of good news for the Prophet ﷺ.

Regarding 'a quittance in the scriptures', Ibn 'Abbas links it to the Preserved Tablet, while others relate it to the books revealed to the prophets. Al-Mawardi presents it as a safeguard against the ruin that befell earlier peoples. Ibn 'Ashur adds that the Hour mentioned next is the term of their punishment, which is more severe than that of this world.

This verse announces that the multitude of the Quraysh will be routed and will turn their backs in flight, a promise of victory for the Prophet ﷺ over his opponents. The commentators agree that the promise was fulfilled at Badr. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, al-Rabi' ibn Anas and Ibn Zayd report that it refers to the gathering at Badr, and according to 'Umar, 'Ikrima and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab the Prophet ﷺ recited it while leaping in his armour on the day of Badr. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and others relate that Abu Jahl had said, "We are a victorious host", and that the verse was revealed in reply. Ibn 'Ashur holds that the defeat occurred at Badr and again at the Battle of the Trench, when the confederates fled by night. Opinions differ on when it was revealed: Ibn 'Abbas and most scholars treat it as Meccan, while others, as noted by Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Samani, consider it Medinan. The readings differ between passive and active forms and between singular and plural forms of the word for back, which most take as a collective noun for the sake of rhyme, while al-Zamakhshari reads it in the plural. Most exegetes draw from this a warning of punishment in this world before the next, since, as Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri explain, the Hour is their appointed time, and its torment is more grievous and more bitter.

This verse states that the idolaters who denied the resurrection and trusted in their strength will not escape punishment: the Hour, meaning the Day of Resurrection, is their true appointed time, and it is more calamitous and more bitter than any punishment in this world. Commentators link it to the defeat foretold for their army. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir take it as an allusion to the defeat at Badr, which they describe as lighter than the torment of the Hereafter; al-Razi holds that the warning covers both this life and the next. On the meaning of the words, al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain "adhā" as more severe and grievous, al-Razi as the greatest of calamities, and Ibn 'Ashur as the calamity of eternal abiding in the Fire. "Amarr" refers to bitterness: al-Mawardi gives it as the sharpest taste or what penetrates most deeply, while al-Razi reads it as lasting. Most hold the surah to be Meccan. Across the wider passage, the majority explain that the guilty are in error and torment in this world and in the Fire in the next, dragged on their faces and told to taste the touch of Saqar.

This verse states that the criminals, meaning the disbelievers and those who denied the messengers, are misguided and in confusion in this world, and that on the Day of Judgment they will face a blazing fire, being dragged into it on their faces while being told in reproach: taste the touch of Saqar. Most commentators understand the criminals to be the disbelievers, but Ibn Abbas and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, as reported by al-Tabari, also see the Qadariyya who denied divine decree, relying on several traditions. Al-Tabari explains the misguidance as turning away from the truth and the sa'ar as burning in the hardship of falsehood, a view Qatada shares. Others, such as Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Juzayy, record that sa'ar can mean madness, as Ibn Abbas said. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi treat the word taste as a metaphor for feeling pain, al-Razi explaining that tasting is the most complete form of perception. As for the words that We created everything by measure, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy explain them as God's prior knowledge and decree of all things, while Ibn Abbas understands them as the fitting proportion of each thing to its purpose. The commentators agree that the verse warns against sin and affirms God's comprehensive knowledge and determination of all things.

This verse describes the fate of the criminals, meaning those who denied the truth. In this world they are astray from the truth, and in the hereafter they are thrown into a blazing fire. On the day they are dragged through the Fire on their faces, they will be told, as a rebuke, to taste the touch of Saqar, a name of Hell. The commentators agree on the broad sense: the straying belongs to this life and the burning to the next. Ibn 'Abbas explains sa'ar as madness, Qatada as hardship and torment, and al-Dahhak as a fire kindled against them. As to who the criminals are, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy identify them as disbelievers and polytheists, while al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baghawi report that the verse also targets the Qadariyya, those who denied divine decree, citing narrations about the occasion of revelation. On divine decree, Sunni commentators such as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy see in the verse proof that God measured all things and recorded them before they came into being, and Ibn 'Abbas adds that everything has a fitting measure. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi note that the accusative reading of kull shay' shows that God created everything. On how the touch of the Fire is felt, al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take the tasting as a figure of speech for suffering, while al-Razi stresses the intensity of the sensation. Commentators also differ on how the time phrase connects: al-Tabari and Abu al-Su'ud attach it to what precedes, while al-Razi attaches it to the command to taste.

The commentators explain that this verse affirms God created everything in precise measure and by prior decree, so that every event in the universe is determined and recorded before it occurs. It comes in a passage warning the guilty who dispute divine destiny. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others report that it was revealed concerning the Quraysh who argued with the Prophet ﷺ about qadar, and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi saw it as a rebuke aimed at the proponents of unrestricted free will. Scholars such as al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir understand qadar as the decree fixed beforehand in the Preserved Tablet, citing the hadith: everything is by decree, even helplessness and shrewdness. Al-Mawardi offers two meanings: a measure willed by God without excess or deficiency, or a prior and binding judgment. On the grammar of the word 'kull', most readers put it in the accusative, with an implied verb explained by 'khalaqnahu', a reading favoured by the Kufans and al-Nahhas. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi consider it stronger because it extends creation to everything. Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi note that the nominative reading attributed to Abu al-Sammal was used by those who denied divine decree to take it as describing a measure of form or time. Al-Razi argues that the accusative reading serves against the Mu'tazila, since human acts are also created by God. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Qasimi emphasise the wisdom and order governing creation.

The verse says that when God wills something, His command is one word, "Be," and it comes into being as quickly as a glance of the eye, without delay or repetition. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take "one" to mean this single word, while al-Razi sees in it both the swiftness of execution and the uniformity of God's command whether the thing is great or small, and reads the glance comparison as describing the speed of existence rather than of the command itself. The commentators agree that the verse is addressed to the Quraysh, warned that peoples like them were destroyed before. They also agree that all their deeds are recorded: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi place this record in the books of the recording angels, while others place it in the Preserved Tablet. Ibn Abbas, Qatada and al-Dahhak explain the word "mustatar" as written down or recorded. Several reports cited by al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir link these verses to the Qadariyya, who denied divine predestination, and Sunni scholars rely on them to affirm God's prior decree. Al-Zamakhshari reads "kulla shay'in" in the accusative, a choice Abu Hayyan discusses at length. On the word "nahar" in the next verse, al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi take it as rivers of water, wine, honey and milk, while Ibn Jurayj and others take it as light and abundance. The overall meaning remains God's absolute power, a warning to the disbelievers, and a promise to the righteous.

This verse reminds the disbelievers of Quraysh that God destroyed earlier peoples who were like them in their disbelief, and it invites the listener to take warning from their fate. The commentators agree that "ashya'" means their counterparts or like-minded peers in unbelief, and that "muddakir" is one who remembers and takes heed. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi stress the lesson to be drawn, while al-Jalalayn reads the question as a command to remember and be admonished. Al-Razi links the passage to the threat of destruction and to the fact that every deed is recorded. On the meaning of "zubur", opinions differ: al-Tabari, Ibn Zayd and al-Dahhak take it to mean books, al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi refer it to the registers of the recording angels, while al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Zamakhshari identify it with the Preserved Tablet; al-Qurtubi also cites the view that it is the Mother of the Book. As for "mustatar", al-Hasan, Ikrima and Ibn Zayd understand it as "written", whereas Qatada renders it as "preserved". The commentators present these views without deciding between them, and agree that every deed of the earlier peoples, great or small, is recorded until the Day of Reckoning.

The commentators explain that the verse means that everything the earlier peoples, the likes of the Quraysh in disbelief, did, whether good or bad, is recorded against them in the Zubur. They differ on what the Zubur are. Al-Tabari, Ibn Zayd, al-Dahhak and Ibn Kathir take them to be the registers of the recording angels, with al-Tabari also allowing that the Mother of the Book may be meant. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Ibn al-Jawzi, along with Ibn 'Atiyya, refer to the Preserved Tablet or to the angels' registers. Ibn al-Qayyim reports the reconciliation offered by Abu Ishaq: the writing exists in the Preserved Tablet before the act and is recorded again after it, for reward and punishment, and he regards this as the soundest view. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur read the verse as a warning to the present audience: destruction in this world is not the full extent of their punishment, since a reckoning awaits in the hereafter. Al-Razi stresses that everything, small or great, is written, and explains the order of the words by how people usually record small matters first. Al-Shinqiti and Ibn 'Uthaymin affirm that every human deed is written and nothing is forgotten. The commentators thus agree on the core meaning: nothing escapes God's record, and this should prompt reflection and vigilance.

This verse states that everything, small or great, is recorded and written down. Most commentators explain the word mustatar as written or inscribed, among them al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baghawi. Al-Tabari reports from Ibn Abbas that this refers to what is written in the Preserved Tablet. Qatada took it to mean that the record is preserved, and al-Mawardi presents both meanings as two possible views. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud place this writing on the Preserved Tablet, whereas Ibn Juzayy links it to the registers of deeds. Ibn 'Ashur reads it as a figure for God's knowledge and the reckoning that follows from it. Al-Razi explains that mentioning the small first reflects human habits of recording, since one begins with what is easy to retain. Most of these scholars tie the verse to the preceding passage on divine decree and the recording of deeds, and Ibn Kathir cites several hadiths on predestination, though no one decides between the readings. Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Atiyya note an unusual recitation with a doubled ra.

This verse announces that the pious, those who fear God by obeying Him and avoiding what He forbids, will be in gardens and among rivers on the Day of Resurrection. The commentators offered several readings of the word nahar. Ibn Jurayj, quoted by al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, takes it as the rivers of Paradise of water, wine, milk and honey. The singular is explained by the verse ending on that sound and by the collective force of the noun, as al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy note. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir also report al-Dahhak's view that the word means light and spaciousness, supported by a line of Qays ibn al-Khatim and by verses attributed to the Arabs, and al-Tabari adds that it can mean daytime. Ibn Kathir cites a tradition that there is no night in Paradise. Some readers pronounced it nuhur in the plural, a reading al-Tabari and al-Razi regard as weaker.

All agree that the pious will dwell in a maqʻad sidq, a seat of truth where there is no idle talk or sin, in the presence of a mighty Sovereign, God. Ibn al-Qayyim explains that sidq means what is firm, complete and desirable, and that the phrase refers both to the place and to the deeds that lead to it. Al-Razi notes that the preposition in this verse can mean near the river, and that a single great river can be a place of honour for the believers.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the state of the God-fearing, set against the criminals mentioned just before: they will be in gardens and rivers, "in a seat of truth", meaning a righteous assembly free of idle talk and sin, "in the presence of a Sovereign, All-Powerful". There is broad agreement that the "seat" is a pleasing place, marked by truth and perfection. Al-Tabari describes it as an assembly of truth without idle talk or sin, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Abu al-Su'ud and Ibn Juzayy speak of a place that is pleasing. Al-Alusi holds that "truth" may be a metonymy or a metaphor.

The meaning of "truth" is debated. Al-Razi, Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Uthaymin take it as the opposite of falsehood: a place where nothing false exists, or whose account is true. Others, such as al-Alusi, read it as the truth of what the Prophet announced, or as the reward of those who believed and confirmed the messengers.

Nearly all agree that "in the presence of" expresses nearness of rank and honour, not physical closeness, as al-Nasafi, al-Biqa'i and Ibn 'Ashur explain. Al-Biqa'i sees the deliberately indefinite "Sovereign" and "All-Powerful" as a way of signalling a greatness beyond human grasp. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi relate reports about the gatherings of the blessed, whose authenticity is not settled here.

Al-Razi also distinguishes "sitting" from "being seated", the former implying duration and stability.
